    About

    Director’s Message

    Director’s MessageMissionHistoryDirections

    We have what it takes to turn the dream of robots into reality

    Thank you for visiting Seoul National University Robotics Institute. I often think about where a good robot begins. My answer is that it begins not with a technology but with a question. Only when we have decided whose problem we are solving, and which problem, can we design a body and an intelligence to fit it. That is why we set out to build robots for people, not robots that merely resemble people.

    The places where this question matters most are close to home. In a super-aged society, more and more people who need care themselves are caring for someone else. What this reality calls for is not intelligence that stays on a screen but robots that lend real physical help, close to people’s bodies and in the spaces where they live. This is why the Institute’s research centers on robots that support daily life, wearable robots, and medical robots that help with diagnosis and treatment inside the body.

    Robots used this close to people cannot be built with the knowledge of a single field. We have to consider not only how well a robot performs but also the body of the person using it, the environment they live in, and their safety. That is why more than 80 researchers from engineering, medicine, public health, brain and cognitive sciences, clothing and textiles, and the social sciences work together at the Institute. By convergence we do not mean everyone doing the same work toward the same goal. We mean one researcher’s idea being applied in a new way by another, and that result in turn moving yet another line of research.

    A good idea, however, does not by itself become a good robot. A robot gets better through a cycle repeated many times: build it, use it in the field, and feed the problems that surface back into the design. It is hard for a single lab to sustain this cycle on its own. The Institute therefore aims to provide a shared foundation for turning ideas into real robots and testing them, to work with hospitals to confirm that they truly help, and to open a path from research results to commercialization and start-ups.

    Researchers have long said that hardware is hard. A robot does not live in a metaverse where any idea can be realized; it has to work safely and usefully in the real world. That is why building the hardware we call a robot is inherently difficult. To accomplish something this hard, education, research and industry must form an ecosystem in which each feeds the others. Students learn by making things themselves; that experience becomes research; research is put to use in industry; and what is learned there returns to education and research.

    Our selection as a National Research Lab allows us to concentrate on building this ecosystem for the next ten years. We will make the Institute a place that outstanding people seek out on their own. I hope that what none of us could do alone, we can now do together. We look forward to the researchers, students and companies who will build robots for people with us, and to everyone who needs them.

    Kyu-Jin Cho Director, SNU Robotics Institute

    About

    Mission

    Director’s MessageMissionHistoryDirections

    Building a robotics ecosystem where education, research and entrepreneurship drive one another

    SNU Robotics Institute aims to bring together research expertise across disciplines and build an ecosystem in which the outcomes of education and research lead to practical technology applications and new ventures. Through this approach, we seek to become an internationally competitive research institute and to contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of Korea’s robotics industry.

    1. 01

      Creative technologies through interdisciplinary research

      We foster a research environment in which researchers from different fields define and solve problems together. By combining knowledge and research methods across departments and disciplines, we develop robotics technologies that would be difficult to achieve within a single field.

    2. 02

      Technology innovation driven by societal needs

      We pursue technologies that address real needs in society and industry. The requirements of users and application environments inform research planning, and the usefulness of new technologies is validated in the field. This process helps research outcomes translate into practical applications.

    3. 03

      Developing talent through hands-on education

      We establish an educational foundation that enables students to design, build and run experiments themselves. Research equipment, spaces and expertise are connected with education to give students experience in solving real problems. In this way, we develop robotics talent with both theoretical knowledge and practical implementation skills.

    4. 04

      Support from technology development to commercialization and entrepreneurship

      We are building a Lab to Market framework that provides continuous support for the technology development, scale-up and commercialization of research outcomes. Technical staff help advance technologies toward commercial use, while market experts and entrepreneurs identify application markets and business opportunities. Our aim is to connect the development of research technologies with preparations for launching new ventures.

    5. 05

      A research environment where researchers can keep taking on new challenges

      We envision a “Return to RI” support framework that enables researchers to return to the Institute after pursuing entrepreneurship and continue with further research and new initiatives. We aim to reduce the risks of entrepreneurship and bring experience gained in the field back into research and education.

    Education

    Our Approach

    CEDCreative Engineering Design since 1993Creative Engineering Design→

    Educating engineers for the age of AI

    We live in an age when artificial intelligence answers our questions and summarizes knowledge for us. Information has never been easier to obtain, and for that very reason, what it means to truly know something is changing. SNU Robotics Institute believes that in the age of AI, the knowledge that remains one’s own comes from what one has confronted and worked through firsthand.

    That is why our education does not stop at making something by hand. Students define a problem, design their own robots, and then put those robots in a real arena to compete against robots built by their classmates. A design that looked perfect on paper falters in the face of friction, error and the unexpected, and in closing that gap, students learn how to turn an idea into technology that actually works.

    None of this is accomplished alone. Students divide roles, reconcile opinions and, at times, weather failure together. Learning from rivals and joining forces with teammates to push past their limits gives them something no lecture can replace: the firmest foundation for becoming an engineer.

    1. 01ImagineImagine
    2. 02DesignDesign
    3. 03CollaborateCollaborate
    4. 04Make it realMake it real

    Imagine, design, collaborate and make it real. This is the educational philosophy of SNU Robotics Institute. Education like this demands a great deal of time, space and equipment, and the dedication of faculty and teaching assistants. It is by no means an easy path, but to uphold this philosophy we provide our students with hands-on education. It is this conviction that has kept Creative Engineering Design going for more than 30 years since it began in 1993.

    Faculty-founded companies

    Companies founded or co-founded by Institute faculty.

    • Rebodis

      Soft wearable robots worn like clothing. A knee-assist robot is being prepared as the first product.

      Co-founded by Prof. Kyu-Jin ChoFounded 2025↗

      Develops knee X-ray reading AI, surgical planning software and a robot for knee replacement surgery.

      Founded by Prof. Du Hyun RoFounded 2021↗
    • OnePredict

      Builds industrial AI solutions that predict equipment failure risk and remaining useful life.

      Founded by Prof. Byeng D. YounFounded 2016↗
    • SAIGE

      Builds AI vision inspection solutions that find defects on the manufacturing floor.

      Co-founded by Prof. Frank C. ParkFounded 2017↗
    • PROTEINA

      Supports drug discovery and diagnostics with technology for analyzing protein–protein interactions. Listed on KOSDAQ.

      Founded by Prof. Tae-Young YoonFounded 2015↗
    • Cipherome

      Builds a platform that analyzes genomic and clinical data to guide medication choices for each person.

      Co-founded by Prof. Ju Han KimFounded 2015↗

    National Research Lab

    National Research Lab (NRL 2.0)

    Human-Centered Physical AI Robotics Institute

    National Research Laboratory Program

    National Research Lab (NRL 2.0)

    4 · 3Technical Core · Project Group78Faculty (41 participating · 37 affiliated)
    2026–2035Up to ten years of support · the only one in robotics

    Research Goals

    Through this program, SNU Robotics Institute develops foundational technologies for human-centered physical AI by co-designing robot bodies and intelligence. Concentrating all decisions and control in a central AI creates challenges in computation, energy use and response time in complex real-world settings. The project combines embodied physical intelligence, in which materials, structures, contact and deformation contribute to computation and adaptation, with distributed intelligence, in which each part of the robot processes information, learns and cooperates with higher-level intelligence. The goal is to establish design, learning and control principles for robots that adapt to their environments and users.

    Human-centered research addresses both robot capabilities and the conditions in which people use them. Safety, clinical reliability, user autonomy and social acceptance are considered and assessed from the design stage. Digital twins of robot–human–environment interactions complement physical experiments to evaluate performance and practical applicability.

    Research framework

    The Technical Cores (TCs) develop foundational technologies shared across applications. The Project Groups (PGs) define use environments and research requirements, then apply and evaluate these technologies.

    TC 1MORPHI BodyAdaptive robot bodies using the physical properties of materials and structuresTC 2MOSAIC IntelligenceDistributed intelligence coordinating local and global modulesTC 3Digital TwinRobot–human–environment models for design, learning and evaluationTC 4Human ValueAssessment of safety, clinical reliability and social acceptancePG 1Life CompanionEveryday assistance robots that adapt to user intentions and changing living environmentsPG 2WearableWearable robots that assist or augment movement, strength and balancePG 3Intra-BodyRobots and diagnostic or therapeutic interfaces operating inside the human body

    Validation and commercialization

    The program aims to apply shared foundational technologies in real use environments and feed the validation results back into technology development. So that research results do not stay in the lab, we are setting up shared research infrastructure for fabrication, data and computing, and pursuing a Lab-to-Market framework that links industry collaboration, technology commercialization and entrepreneurship.

    National Research Lab

    TC + PG

    Research at the National Research Lab advances on two interlocking axes. The Technical Cores (TCs) develop shared foundational technologies, from the robot’s body and intelligence to digital twins and human values, while the Project Groups (PGs) take on human-centered applications such as everyday assistance, wearable robots and intra-body robots. The PGs pose the problems to be solved, and the TCs provide the technologies that solve them.

    TC 1 MORPHI BodyTC 2 MOSAIC IntelligenceTC 3 Digital TwinTC 4 Human ValuePG 1 Life CompanionPG 2 WearablePG 3 Intra-Body

    Technical Core (TC)

    TC 01 · MORPHI Body

    Adaptive robot materials, structures and physical intelligence

    Why it matters

    Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. This is why robots need materials and structures that themselves distribute forces and comply with their surroundings, going beyond the limits of a fixed body.

    Research approach

    MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with variable structures that change shape and stiffness to suit the environment. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware.

    Key research topics

    • Reconfigurable actuation and structures: joints with actively adjustable shape and stiffness, and bio-inspired artificial muscles
    • Self-sensing skin: soft distributed tactile sensors and systems for monitoring the robot’s physical state
    • Modularity and reliability: shared specifications, plus durability and reliability testing, for low-cost, low-power hardware

    TC 02 · MOSAIC Intelligence

    Cooperative distributed intelligence and continual learning

    Why it matters

    Retraining an entire intelligence system whenever a robot’s body or task environment changes demands substantial time and computing resources. Real-world settings also require immediate responses to contact with people and changes in task conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior.

    Research approach

    Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence studies an architecture in which a higher-level global intelligence coordinates local intelligence for each body part and function. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks.

    Key research topics

    • Autonomous local intelligence: modules that perceive the physical properties of robots, humans and environments and learn movement independently
    • Contextual global intelligence: understanding and predicting situations to coordinate perception and movement modules
    • Continual learning and co-evolution: local and global intelligence learning together and adapting to new environments and missions

    TC 03 · Digital Twin

    Robot–human–environment digital twin

    Why it matters

    Predicting contact between people and robots in changing environments requires multiple physical phenomena to be considered together. Existing digital twins can be fragmented by phenomenon, or face a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computing speed. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation of complex interactions alongside consistent management of diverse data.

    Research approach

    The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. We study how to generate and augment physically consistent data in virtual experiments and connect it with real-world observations for iterative robot design and validation. The aim is an integrated framework that supports everyday assistance, wearable and intra-body robots under their different operating conditions.

    Key research topics

    • Digital twin: high-accuracy, high-speed simulation of complex physical interactions and generation of data for learning and validation
    • Data fabric: generating, augmenting, storing and managing large-scale data in diverse formats while preserving physical consistency and context
    • Infrastructure optimization: integrated software–hardware design for efficient simulation and data processing

    TC 04 · Human Value

    Robot safety, clinical reliability and social acceptance

    Why it matters

    Higher performance alone does not make a robot beneficial or trustworthy. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than only evaluating ethics or usability after development is complete, a framework is needed that reflects and verifies these values from initial design through control and real-world validation.

    Research approach

    Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. The aim is to lay a foundation for comparing and judging robots’ clinical reliability and social acceptance against consistent criteria.

    Key research topics

    • Value-based design: defining indicators for safety, functioning and autonomy and using them in design and validation
    • Real-world validation and stress testing: identifying thresholds of value compromise across interaction scenarios and explaining the basis for each judgment
    • Shared criteria and design feedback: studying a Human Value API and reliability criteria, and feeding evaluation results into control and design improvements

    A Hands-on Robot Design Course

    Creative Engineering Design

    A signature engineering course of the SNU College of Engineering, running for more than 30 years since 1993

    About the Course

    Creative Engineering Design is a project-based course in which first-year students in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University work in teams to design and build their own robots. First introduced in 1993 by the late Professor Chong Nam Chu, it has continued for more than 30 years and has become a signature engineering course at the SNU College of Engineering. Students conceive robots that carry out a given mission, then build and test them under set constraints, solving problems as they go and developing creativity, teamwork and engineering problem-solving skills along the way. The course content has changed steadily to reflect advances in technology, and since 2024 it has used wireless remote controllers as a foundation for teaching AI robot architecture.

    DesignFirst-year students turn their own ideas into a robot design
    BuildTeams make and test their robots by hand
    CompeteRobots face off at Robocon, the end-of-semester contest

    Curriculum

    Creative Engineering Design

    This course aims to develop a basic sense of design and fabrication, as well as creativity, through hands-on practice in designing and building a variety of assigned objects. Intended for first-year students who have not yet formed a clear concept of engineering, it has students build products themselves from specified materials and compete with them, so that they can experience the meaning of engineering with genuine interest. The products take many forms, such as mechanisms and structures, that together reflect the characteristics of various engineering fields. The course is structured so that students with little experience in coding or hardware can learn step by step from the introductory stage.

    Building on Internet of Things (IoT) technology, which is widely used across industrial devices and home appliances including automobiles, robots and smartphones, students learn the basic structure of microcontrollers (Arduino, 32-bit MCUs, etc.), collect data through sensors for temperature, humidity, light, sound, motion and images, and learn the principles of connecting and controlling output devices such as displays and motors. They then connect objects through wired and wireless communication and implement on-device AI (TinyML), which learns from the collected data and runs inference directly on the device. In this way, they complete the entire process from sensing to reasoning and action as a single integrated system, extending to Physical AI—artificial intelligence that perceives, reasons about and acts upon the real world on its own. By combining theory with hands-on practice, the course can also be linked with other engineering design courses that range from fundamentals to prototype development.

    The course consists of two hours of lecture and two hours of lab each week. During the first six weeks, lectures on basic design principles, kinematics and fabrication methods are combined with robot programming practice and fabrication. In week 7, the purpose and rules of the robots that students will design and build are announced, and in week 12 the main competition is held with the robots each team has freely designed and built within the given rules, using the materials and tools provided.

    Mechanical System Design and Robot Programming

    A required preparatory course that students take before Creative Engineering Design.

    This lecture focuses on learning the initial skillset for mechanical system design, covering both hardware and software aspects. Starting from CAD, the class covers basic programming, including python, C/C++, and Matlab. Most importantly, the course goes beyond learning programming languages: students carry their programs through to deployment on hardware.

    1. Weeks 1–6Lectures on design principles, kinematics and fabrication; robot programming practice
    2. Week 7Robot purpose and rules announced
    3. Week 12Main Robocon match

    SNU Robocon

    Robocon

    The course culminates in Robocon, a team competition in which every student competes with the robot they built in class. The winning team goes on to represent Korea at an international Robocon competition.
